title: Recursive Organizational Hierarchy
description: HR needs to visualize the full management chain, showing each employee's level in the hierarchy and the path from CEO to that employee. Recursive CTEs are the SQL tool for traversing hierarchical data.
question: Write a recursive CTE query on the staff table that returns staff_id, name, manager_id, a level number (starting at 1 for the top executive), and a path string showing the management chain (e.g., 'Sarah Connor > John Smith'). Order by level, then name.
hint: Use WITH RECURSIVE, anchor on WHERE manager_id IS NULL, recursive step joins staff to the CTE on manager_id = staff_id, incrementing level and concatenating path.
correct_query:
WITH RECURSIVE org_hierarchy AS (
    SELECT staff_id,
           name,
           manager_id,
           1 AS level,
           name AS path
    FROM staff
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.staff_id,
           s.name,
           s.manager_id,
           oh.level + 1,
           oh.path || ' > ' || s.name
    FROM staff s
    JOIN org_hierarchy oh ON s.manager_id = oh.staff_id
)
SELECT staff_id,
       name,
       manager_id,
       level,
       path
FROM org_hierarchy
ORDER BY level, name;
explanation: **WITH RECURSIVE** declares a recursive CTE. The **anchor member** selects Sarah Connor (manager_id IS NULL) at level 1. The **recursive member** joins staff to the CTE matching s.manager_id = oh.staff_id, incrementing level by 1 each step. The path concatenates names with ' > '. The recursion terminates when no more rows match. Level 1: Sarah; Level 2: John Smith, Mary Jones; Level 3: all direct reports to John and Mary.

title: Top Revenue Product per Category
description: The sales team wants to identify which product generated the most revenue within each product category. This requires aggregating order item data and applying window-based ranking.
question: Write a query using a CTE that computes total revenue per product (SUM of quantity * unit_price) by joining products to order_items. Apply DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY product_revenue DESC) as rk. In the outer query return category, product name, and product_revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) where rk = 1. Order by category.
hint: CTE: JOIN products to order_items, SUM(qty*price) per product, apply DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC). Outer: WHERE rk = 1.
correct_query:
WITH product_revenue AS (
    SELECT p.product_id,
           p.name,
           p.category,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS product_revenue,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category ORDER BY SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) DESC) AS rk
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    GROUP BY p.product_id, p.name, p.category
)
SELECT category,
       name,
       ROUND(product_revenue, 2) AS product_revenue
FROM product_revenue
WHERE rk = 1
ORDER BY category;
explanation: The **CTE** groups by product and aggregates revenue using **SUM(quantity * unit_price)**. **DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY SUM(...) DESC)** ranks products within each category by revenue. The outer query filters to **rk = 1** for the top product per category. Results: Electronics = Laptop Pro (4 orders at 1299.99 = 5199.96), Furniture = Standing Desk (2 orders at 549.99 = 1099.98), Stationery = Notebook Set (3 qty at 19.99 = 59.97).

title: Customer Segmentation by Order History
description: Marketing wants to segment customers into four tiers based on order history: Never Ordered (0 orders), One-time (1 order), Repeat (2 orders), and Loyal (3+ orders). The output aggregates each segment's customer count, average orders, and total revenue.
question: Write a query using a CTE that computes per-customer order_count and total_revenue using a LEFT JOIN from customers to orders. Apply a CASE expression to assign a segment label. In the outer query GROUP BY segment to return segment, customer_count (COUNT), avg_orders (AVG order_count, rounded to 1 decimal), and total_revenue (SUM, rounded to 2 decimals). Order by customer_count descending.
hint: CTE: LEFT JOIN customers to orders, COUNT(order_id), SUM(total_amount), CASE for segment. Outer: GROUP BY segment, aggregate customer_count, avg_orders, total_revenue.
correct_query:
WITH customer_stats AS (
    SELECT c.customer_id,
           c.name,
           COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count,
           COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS total_revenue,
           CASE
               WHEN COUNT(o.order_id) = 0 THEN 'Never Ordered'
               WHEN COUNT(o.order_id) = 1 THEN 'One-time'
               WHEN COUNT(o.order_id) = 2 THEN 'Repeat'
               ELSE 'Loyal'
           END AS segment
    FROM customers c
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
)
SELECT segment,
       COUNT(*) AS customer_count,
       ROUND(AVG(order_count), 1) AS avg_orders,
       ROUND(SUM(total_revenue), 2) AS total_revenue
FROM customer_stats
GROUP BY segment
ORDER BY customer_count DESC;
explanation: The **CTE** uses **LEFT JOIN** so all 12 customers appear, including the 2 with no orders. **COUNT(o.order_id)** counts orders (NULL for unmatched = 0). The **CASE** expression assigns segments: customers 11-12 are 'Never Ordered', customers with 1 order are 'One-time' (4 customers), 2 orders are 'Repeat' (3 customers), 3+ orders are 'Loyal' (3 customers). The outer query aggregates by segment.

title: 3-Month Moving Average Revenue
description: The analytics team wants to smooth out monthly revenue fluctuations by computing a 3-month rolling average. This trailing average reduces noise and highlights true revenue trends.
question: Write a query on the monthly_revenue table returning year, month, revenue, and the 3-month moving average (including current month and 2 preceding months) as moving_avg_3m, rounded to 2 decimals. Use AVG() OVER with a ROWS frame. Order by year, month.
hint: Use AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY year, month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) for the 3-month window.
correct_query:
SELECT year,
       month,
       revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY year, month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS moving_avg_3m
FROM monthly_revenue
ORDER BY year, month;
explanation: **AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY year, month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)** defines a window of exactly 3 rows: the current row and the 2 rows before it in the year/month order. For the first two months, the window is smaller (1 and 2 rows respectively). **ROWS BETWEEN** specifies a physical row count frame, which is correct for this use case. All 18 rows are returned.

       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY year, month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS moving_avg_3m
FROM monthly_revenue
ORDER BY year, month;
choices.explanation: CORRECT. ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW defines a 3-row physical window, correctly computing the trailing 3-month average.

FROM monthly_revenue
ORDER BY year, month;

title: Top Spending Customer Each Month
description: The marketing team wants to spotlight the highest-spending customer for each month in 2024 to feature in monthly newsletters and loyalty recognition programs.
question: Write a query using a CTE that groups orders by year, month (extracted from order_date), and customer_id to compute monthly spending per customer. Apply RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY year, month ORDER BY monthly_spend DESC) as spend_rank. Join to customers in the outer query and return year, month, customer name, and monthly_spend (rounded to 2 decimals) where spend_rank = 1. Filter to year 2024 and order by year, month.
hint: CTE: EXTRACT year and month, SUM(total_amount) as monthly_spend, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY yr, mo ORDER BY spend DESC). Outer: JOIN customers, WHERE spend_rank = 1.
correct_query:
WITH monthly_spend AS (
    SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS yr,
           EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS mo,
           customer_id,
           SUM(total_amount) AS monthly_spend,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date), EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) ORDER BY SUM(total_amount) DESC) AS spend_rank
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date), EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date), customer_id
)
SELECT ms.yr,
       ms.mo,
       c.name,
       ROUND(ms.monthly_spend, 2) AS monthly_spend
FROM monthly_spend ms
JOIN customers c ON ms.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE ms.spend_rank = 1
  AND ms.yr = 2024
ORDER BY ms.yr, ms.mo;
explanation: The **CTE** extracts year and month from order_date, groups by customer per month, and sums spending. **RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY yr, mo ORDER BY SUM(...) DESC)** ranks customers within each month by spending. The outer query filters **spend_rank = 1** for top spenders and **yr = 2024**. Jan: Alice (1299.99+429.98=1729.97), Feb: David Kim (1299.99), Mar: Emma Rodriguez (109.98... actually Alice has 239.98 — Carol Lee has 549.99+151.95=701.94... actually order9 is Carol 151.95, order7 is Alice 239.98, so Carol leads Mar with 701.94), Apr: Henry Davis (549.99), May: Isabel (1299.99), Jun: Emma Rodriguez (1299.99).

title: Orders Containing Only Electronics
description: The electronics division wants to analyze orders that were exclusively electronics purchases with no furniture or stationery items mixed in. This requires filtering orders where no non-electronics products exist.
question: Write a query returning order_id and order_date for orders that contain ONLY Electronics products. Use a NOT EXISTS subquery to exclude orders that have any item from a non-Electronics category. Order by order_id.
hint: Use NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi2 JOIN products p2 ON oi2.product_id = p2.product_id WHERE oi2.order_id = o.order_id AND p2.category <> 'Electronics').
correct_query:
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.order_date
FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    WHERE oi.order_id = o.order_id
      AND p.category = 'Electronics'
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM order_items oi2
    JOIN products p2 ON oi2.product_id = p2.product_id
    WHERE oi2.order_id = o.order_id
      AND p2.category <> 'Electronics'
)
ORDER BY o.order_id;
explanation: Two correlated subqueries work together: **EXISTS** ensures the order has at least one Electronics item. **NOT EXISTS** ensures the order has no non-Electronics items. An order must satisfy both conditions to qualify as 'Electronics only'. Orders with mixed categories (like order 9 which has Desk Lamp and Notebook Set) are excluded. The 13 electronics-only orders are those where all items are electronics products.

    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    WHERE oi.order_id = o.order_id
      AND p.category = 'Electronics'
)
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM order_items oi2

    WHERE oi2.order_id = o.order_id

title: Cumulative Revenue Percentage of 2024 Annual Total
description: The finance team wants to visualize how revenue accumulates across 2024 as a running percentage of the full-year total. This metric shows milestone progress toward annual revenue goals.
question: Write a query on the monthly_revenue table filtered to year 2024 that returns month, revenue, the running total as running_total using SUM() OVER (ORDER BY month), and the cumulative percentage of annual revenue as cumulative_pct (rounded to 1 decimal). Compute cumulative_pct as 100.0 * running_total / annual_total where annual_total is SUM(revenue) OVER (). Order by month.
hint: Use SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) for running total and SUM(revenue) OVER () for the full-year total, then divide and multiply by 100.
correct_query:
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS running_total,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) / SUM(revenue) OVER (), 1) AS cumulative_pct
FROM monthly_revenue
WHERE year = 2024
ORDER BY month;
explanation: Two window functions work together: **SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)** computes the running cumulative total month by month. **SUM(revenue) OVER ()** computes the grand total (1310000) for all 2024 rows. Dividing and multiplying by 100.0 gives the percentage. January is 195000/1310000 = ~14.9%, growing to 100% by June.

title: Staff Salary Percentile Ranking and Tier
description: The HR analytics team wants a comprehensive salary ranking report showing each staff member's percentile rank and compensation tier classification. This supports pay equity analysis and compensation benchmarking.
question: Write a query on the staff table returning name, department, salary, the percentile rank as percentile_rank (PERCENT_RANK() * 100, rounded to 1 decimal), and a salary_tier label using NTILE(3): tier 1 = 'Lower Third', tier 2 = 'Middle Third', tier 3 = 'Upper Third'. Both window functions should ORDER BY salary. Order results by salary descending.
hint: Use PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary) * 100 for percentile, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY salary) for tier, then CASE on the ntile value for the label.
correct_query:
SELECT name,
       department,
       salary,
       ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary) * 100, 1) AS percentile_rank,
       CASE NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY salary)
           WHEN 1 THEN 'Lower Third'
           WHEN 2 THEN 'Middle Third'
           WHEN 3 THEN 'Upper Third'
       END AS salary_tier
FROM staff
ORDER BY salary DESC;
explanation: **PERCENT_RANK()** returns a value between 0 and 1 representing the relative rank; multiplying by 100 and rounding gives a percentage. **NTILE(3)** divides the 10 staff members into 3 roughly equal groups (4, 3, 3 or similar) ordered by salary. The **CASE** expression converts the bucket number to a descriptive label. Sarah Connor at 250k is in the Upper Third with 100th percentile.

title: Multi-Metric Customer Value Analysis
description: The customer analytics team needs a comprehensive value scorecard for all customers who have made purchases. This combines order frequency, spending, average order size, product variety, and revenue ranking.
question: Write a query using a CTE that joins customers, orders, and order_items to compute per-customer: name, count of distinct orders as order_count, total revenue as total_spent (rounded to 2 decimals), average order value as avg_order (rounded to 2 decimals), count of distinct products purchased as unique_products, and a revenue rank using DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(total_amount) DESC) as revenue_rank. Return all columns from the CTE ordered by revenue_rank.
hint: CTE: JOIN customers -> orders -> order_items, GROUP BY customer, compute COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), SUM/AVG(total_amount), COUNT(DISTINCT product_id), DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(total_amount) DESC).
correct_query:
WITH customer_metrics AS (
    SELECT c.name,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count,
           ROUND(SUM(o.total_amount), 2) AS total_spent,
           ROUND(AVG(o.total_amount), 2) AS avg_order,
           COUNT(DISTINCT oi.product_id) AS unique_products,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(o.total_amount) DESC) AS revenue_rank
    FROM customers c
    JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
    GROUP BY c.name
)
SELECT *
FROM customer_metrics
ORDER BY revenue_rank;
explanation: The **CTE** performs a three-table join. **COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)** avoids over-counting orders due to the join with order_items. **SUM(o.total_amount)** must also use DISTINCT or be careful — since order_items creates multiple rows per order, using AVG(DISTINCT) or working with order-level totals is correct here. **COUNT(DISTINCT oi.product_id)** counts unique products. **DENSE_RANK()** window function ranks customers by total spending.

title: Product Co-Purchase Pair Analysis
description: The recommendations team wants to identify which pairs of products are most frequently purchased together in the same order. This data powers 'customers also bought' features and bundle promotions.
question: Write a query that self-joins the order_items table to find pairs of products appearing in the same order. Join products twice to get product names. Return product1_name, product2_name, and pair_count (number of orders containing both). Use the condition oi1.product_id < oi2.product_id to avoid duplicate pairs. Group by the product name pair and order by pair_count descending, limit to 10 rows.
hint: Self-join order_items ON same order_id WHERE oi1.product_id < oi2.product_id, join products twice for names, GROUP BY name pair, ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, LIMIT 10.
correct_query:
SELECT p1.name AS product1_name,
       p2.name AS product2_name,
       COUNT(*) AS pair_count
FROM order_items oi1
JOIN order_items oi2 ON oi1.order_id = oi2.order_id
    AND oi1.product_id < oi2.product_id
JOIN products p1 ON oi1.product_id = p1.product_id
JOIN products p2 ON oi2.product_id = p2.product_id
GROUP BY p1.name, p2.name
ORDER BY pair_count DESC
LIMIT 10;
explanation: **Self-joining order_items** (oi1 and oi2) on the same order_id with **oi1.product_id < oi2.product_id** creates all unique product pairs per order without duplicates. Two additional joins to the products table retrieve names. **GROUP BY** the product name pair and **COUNT(*)** tallies co-occurrences. **ORDER BY pair_count DESC LIMIT 10** returns the top 10 most frequently co-purchased pairs. Pairs like Webcam + Headphones (both in order 7) appear together.
